findings.title: Full access key is not removed on ownership change
findings.description: The vulnerability arises because the full access key associated with the previous owner is not removed when ownership of the contract is transferred. This design flaw allows the former owner to retain control over the contract via the full access key, which grants privileges such as redeploying the contract or transferring funds. The root cause is the lack of cleanup logic during ownership transfer to revoke the old owner's full access key. An attacker (the previous owner) could exploit this by using their retained full access key to perform unauthorized operations after ownership has nominally changed. The impact includes a compromise of contract integrity and potential loss of control or funds, as the new owner does not have exclusive authority.

findings.title: Mismatched Variable Names
findings.description: This issue stems from inconsistent variable naming across related functions in the pausable plugin, specifically using '__check_paused' in one function and 'check_paused' in another. The mismatch prevents the correct compilation of user code when attempting to use certain macro features, as the compiler treats them as different variables. The root cause is a lack of consistency in variable naming within generated code. An attacker could potentially exploit this by crafting malicious inputs or causing deployment failures, though the primary impact is denial of service through failed compilation. This undermines developer trust and usability, preventing correct implementation of pausing logic.

findings.title: Timelock behind up_deploy_code
findings.description: The up_deploy_code function allows immediate deployment of new contract code without any time delay, enabling a malicious owner to instantly deploy harmful updates. The root cause is the absence of a timelock mechanism that would delay code deployment, giving users time to react. An attacker (malicious or compromised owner) could exploit this by staging and deploying malicious code that drains user funds immediately after users have invested. The impact includes direct financial loss to users, as they are not given sufficient time to withdraw their assets before the malicious code is activated.

findings.title: Lack of State Migration and State Integrality Check
findings.description: The contract lacks a state migration interface, meaning that when a contract is upgraded with new fields (e.g., adding a 'counter2' attribute), the existing state cannot be deserialized correctly. This leads to a denial of service because the contract fails upon attempting to read its state after an upgrade. The root cause is the absence of a migration function to transform old state formats into new ones. An attacker could exploit this by triggering an upgrade with incompatible state, rendering the contract unusable. The impact is a complete halt in contract operations, preventing users from accessing their funds or interacting with the system.

findings.title: Improper Full Access Key Fallback Design
findings.description: The contract allows the owner to attach a full access key, which grants more privileges than the contract owner itself, including the ability to transfer NEAR tokens and deploy new contracts. The root cause is a flawed design that elevates the owner's capabilities beyond intended access controls by allowing them to create full access keys. This creates a privilege escalation vector where the owner can gain excessive control, potentially misusing these powers. The impact is an increased attack surface where the contract owner can act beyond the expected scope, undermining the principle of least privilege and enabling misuse of the contract.

findings.title: Pausable contract management should be handled by AccessControl plugin instead of the owner
findings.description: Currently, only the contract owner can pause or unpause the contract, creating a single point of failure. If the owner's account is compromised or becomes unavailable, the contract cannot be paused in an emergency. The root cause is centralized control over critical functionality. This lack of distributed control reduces accountability and transparency, as no other stakeholders can intervene. An attacker could exploit a compromised owner key to prevent pausing during an attack or to maliciously pause the contract. The impact includes reduced resilience and potential loss of availability or security during critical events.

findings.title: No way to remove access key
findings.description: The plugin does not provide a method to remove a previously added access key. If the private key associated with an access key is leaked, there is no way to revoke it, leaving the contract vulnerable. The root cause is the absence of an owner-only function to remove access keys. An attacker who gains access to a leaked key could exploit this to perform unauthorized actions on the contract. The impact is prolonged exposure to compromise, as the contract remains accessible to unauthorized parties even after detection of a leak.

findings.title: Unchecked Removal of the Paused_Key
findings.description: The pa_unpause_feature() function does not verify whether the key being removed actually exists. The root cause is the lack of a check on the return value of the key removal operation. This can mislead project managers into believing an action succeeded when it did not, potentially leading to incorrect assumptions about the contract's state. An attacker could exploit this by feeding invalid keys and observing behavior to infer internal state or cause confusion in operational procedures. The impact is operational unreliability and potential for human error in contract management.

findings.title: Lack of Macro Attributes for Pausable Derivation
findings.description: Users cannot customize the storage key used by the Pausable macro, limiting flexibility in contract design. The root cause is the lack of support for configurable attributes in the macro definition. This leads to compilation errors when users attempt to set custom storage keys, reducing usability. An attacker could exploit this by forcing developers into suboptimal designs or causing deployment failures. The impact is reduced developer control and potential for errors in contract configuration due to inflexible tooling.

findings.title: Staging code is not removed
findings.description: The staged code (upstage code) is not removed after deployment, unnecessarily consuming contract storage. The root cause is the absence of cleanup logic post-deployment. While not directly exploitable for fund theft, this inefficiency increases storage costs and bloats the contract state. An attacker could exploit this by encouraging repeated staging to exhaust storage, indirectly increasing operational costs. The impact is economic inefficiency and higher long-term maintenance costs for the contract.

findings.title: Unnecessary Clone
findings.description: The code unnecessarily clones data by returning Vec<u8> instead of 'static [u8], leading to redundant memory copies. The root cause is inefficient return type choices in functions. This increases gas consumption during execution. An attacker could exploit this by triggering these functions repeatedly to inflate transaction costs. The impact is higher operational gas fees and reduced performance, affecting user experience and economic efficiency.

findings.title: Question about the design purpose of the Full Access Key Fallback
findings.description: The Full Access Key Fallback mechanism contradicts best practices by allowing full access keys on contracts, which undermines decentralization. The root cause is a design choice that permits FAKs, which can be used to redeploy the contract or steal funds. This leads to extra gas consumption and security risks. An attacker could exploit the presence of a FAK to take over the contract. The impact includes reduced trust in contract immutability and increased centralization risk, contrary to smart contract security principles.

findings.title: Missing documentation for admins being able to remove other admins in ACL
findings.description: The functionality allowing admins to revoke other admins in the same group is not properly documented. The root cause is insufficient documentation in the codebase. This lack of clarity can lead to confusion among developers and auditors about access control behavior. An attacker could exploit this ambiguity to escalate privileges or bypass expected controls. The impact is reduced transparency and potential for misconfiguration due to unclear permission models.

findings.title: Replace default panic with near-sdk panic
findings.description: The code uses the default Rust panic function instead of the NEAR SDK's panic handler, which can lead to unstable behavior and poor error handling. The root cause is the use of standard panic instead of a chain-optimized one. This can make debugging difficult and lead to unpredictable contract behavior. An attacker could exploit this by triggering panics to disrupt contract operation. The impact is reduced reliability and harder recovery from errors, affecting overall system stability.

findings.title: revoke_super_admin_unchecked not exposed through near bindgen
findings.description: The revoke_super_admin_unchecked function is not exposed via near bindgen, making it inaccessible from external interfaces. The root cause is a missing attribute or macro annotation for external exposure. This prevents intended administrative functions from being used, potentially leaving super admin privileges unrevoked. An attacker could exploit this by maintaining unauthorized super admin access. The impact is a failure in access control management and potential persistence of excessive privileges.

findings.title: Open to-dos
findings.description: Multiple TODO comments are present in the codebase, indicating unfinished work or unresolved issues. The root cause is incomplete development or lack of follow-up on technical debt. These TODOs can reveal attack surfaces or areas of weakness to adversaries. An attacker could exploit known TODOs to target unimplemented security checks or edge cases. The impact is increased risk from incomplete logic and exposure of internal development challenges to external observers.

findings.title: Missing documentation for the case of using Upgradable to patch a vulnerability
findings.description: The up_stage_code function stores new code before deployment, which is visible on-chain. If used to patch a critical vulnerability, attackers can inspect the staged code to infer the existing flaw and exploit it before deployment. The root cause is the lack of encryption or obfuscation for staged upgrades. An attacker could exploit this by monitoring up_stage_code to reverse-engineer vulnerabilities in the current version. The impact is accelerated exploitation of known issues, reducing the window for safe patching and increasing risk during critical updates.
